title: The Memory Theatre: Southsea to the Warburg, and the Hermetic Tradition Recovered
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Southsea, the youngest of four
stops.date_confidence: Day attested by Wikipedia and by Trapp's British Academy memoir; one secondary encyclopedia gives 29 November, a one-day discrepancy left unresolved here.
stops.campa: In a naval town at the end of the century a fourth child is born to James Alfred Yates, constructor to the Royal Navy, and to his wife Hannah, in a house within sound of the dockyard. They call her Frances Amelia. Her father builds ships for a service about to rebuild itself entirely around the dreadnought; her mother keeps a household that will be packed and unpacked a dozen times before the girl is twenty. There is an older brother, Jimmy, and two sisters, Hannah and Ruby. Nobody in the family has been to a university.
suggested_refs: Southsea and the Portsmouth naval dockyard, the family's first address
sources: J. B. Trapp, 'Frances Amelia Yates 1899-1981', Proceedings of the British Academy 120 (2003), p. 528

stops.name: Chatham Dockyard, the first transfer
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by Wikipedia; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: James Yates is transferred to the Royal Dockyard at Chatham and the household follows him down the Medway, the first of the moves that will shape his daughter's childhood. Frances is two. She will not remember Portsmouth. What she does remember, and sets down in old age in fragments titled by place name, is a succession of rented houses in towns chosen by the Admiralty rather than by anyone in the family, and a mother who taught her at home because there was rarely time to enrol her anywhere.
suggested_refs: Yates's late 'Autobiographical Fragments', whose pieces are titled by place and year

stops.name: Govan, the dreadnought yards on the Clyde
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the Glasgow move to 1903; the December precision is Trapp's alone and is not independently attested. The coordinate is the Govan shipbuilding reach of the Clyde, not Glasgow city centre; the family's own house was north of the river at Kelvinside.
stops.campa: A second transfer sends the family north to the Clyde, where James Yates takes charge of superintending dreadnought construction in the Glasgow yards. From the Govan bank the great hulls go down the ways into the river. The Yateses settle across the water on the north side, at Kelvinside, and stay eight years, longer than they stay anywhere else. Frances is four when they arrive and eleven when they go. She is taught at home and reads whatever the house holds.
suggested_refs: The Clyde shipbuilding yards at Govan during the dreadnought programme

stops.name: Hillhead, a year at Laurel Bank School
stops.date_confidence: Attendance attested by Wikipedia to 1910-1911; the September start is inferred from the school year. Coordinate corrected to the school's Lilybank Terrace site in Hillhead; the research pool's 55.8656,-4.2652 falls in the city centre, about 1.9 km away.
stops.campa: For a little over a year she is sent to Laurel Bank School in Hillhead, one of the few stretches of formal schooling in a childhood otherwise conducted at the kitchen table. She is eleven. The classroom does not take, and the family is about to move again in any case. Everything she will later know of French, Italian, Latin, palaeography and the reading of state papers she teaches herself or is taught by correspondence. There is no school certificate at the end of any of it.
suggested_refs: Laurel Bank School, Lilybank Terrace, Hillhead, Glasgow

stops.name: Ingleton, the farmhouse after the retirement
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia attests the Ingleton farmhouse and the sequence Llandrindod Wells, Ripon, Harrogate; the months are unknown and the dates are approximate, given as c.1911-1913 in the source.
stops.campa: Her father retires from the Navy and the family, no longer moved by the Admiralty, begins moving on its own account: a farmhouse near Ingleton under the Yorkshire fells, then Llandrindod Wells in the Welsh hills, then Ripon, then Harrogate. Frances is twelve, thirteen, fourteen. She is educated by her mother and her sisters and by whatever the local subscription library holds. Her brother Jimmy, the one on whom the family's hopes rest, is at school being prepared for Oxford.
suggested_refs: The itinerant addresses of 1911-1918: Ingleton, Llandrindod Wells, Ripon, Harrogate, Oxton

stops.name: Harrogate, the news about Jimmy
stops.date_confidence: The death of her brother in 1915 is attested by Wikipedia; the month is unknown and defaulted. The place is this stop's weakest element: a soldier killed in action in 1915 died on active service abroad, and the family's own address that year is uncertain between Harrogate and Oxton. The stop is pinned where the family most probably received the news, not where he died.
stops.campa: Jimmy Yates is killed in action in the second year of the war. He had passed into Oxford; he was the son, and the plan. What the family does with the loss is transfer the whole weight of its expectation onto the youngest daughter, who is fifteen and has had perhaps two years of school in her life. Trapp, writing her memoir for the British Academy nearly a century later, dates the making of Frances Yates the scholar to this death. Where her brother fell, the record reached here does not say.
suggested_refs: Commonwealth War Graves Commission records for James S. Yates, not consulted in this pass

stops.name: Oxton, the examination she fails
stops.date_confidence: The Oxton residence is attested by Wikipedia for c.1916-1918; the Oxford entrance failure is Trapp's, dated only to c.1919. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the village of Oxton on the Wirral; the research pool's 53.3547,-3.0631 lands 3 to 4 km south-west, around Prenton.
stops.campa: On the Wirral, at Oxton above Birkenhead, the family comes to something like rest, and the war ends. Frances is nineteen, with no school certificate, no coach, and no money for a university. She sits the Oxford entrance examination her brother had passed, and fails it. There is no second attempt. The household has no funds for one, and the daughter is not the son. She begins looking instead at what the University of London permits an external candidate to do from a rented room.
suggested_refs: Oxton, Wirral, the family's last northern address

stops.name: Worthing, four years of correspondence
stops.date_confidence: Trapp dates the Worthing years c.1919-1923; the geography lens could not confirm Worthing from a second independent source. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: From a rented house at Worthing she assembles a degree out of almost nothing: correspondence courses in French, a reading list, occasional classes at University College when the fare to London can be found, and four years of her own discipline. She is registered as an external student of a university that examines candidates it does not teach. Nobody supervises her. She takes the family's French holidays as language practice and works through the sixteenth century alone, at the rate a person works who has no one to impress.
suggested_refs: The University of London external degree system, which examined candidates it did not teach

stops.name: Gower Street, first-class honours and the MA
stops.date_confidence: BA 1924 and MA 1926 attested by Wikipedia and Trapp; months unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The stop compresses both degrees at the same address.
stops.campa: She takes the London BA in French with first-class honours, an external candidate who has been inside the university buildings only for occasional classes, and is then admitted as an internal student for the MA under Louis Brandin and F. Y. Eccles. The thesis is on French social drama of the sixteenth century and is finished in 1926. She is twenty-six. Nobody else in the family holds a degree. She has no post to go to, and no institution that owes her anything at all.
suggested_refs: University College London, Gower Street, where she read French under Brandin and Eccles

stops.name: Claygate, the New House on Coverts Road
stops.date_confidence: Purchase attested to 1925 by Trapp and Wikipedia; month unknown. Coordinate corrected to Coverts Road, Claygate KT10 0JY per OSM at 51.3567,-0.3380; the research pool's 51.3667,-0.3333 lies about 1.2 km north-east, outside the village.
stops.campa: The family buys The New House in Coverts Road, Claygate, a Surrey village on the line into Waterloo, and Frances Yates lives in it for fifty-six years. The house is chosen partly for her: from Claygate she can reach the British Museum Reading Room or the Public Record Office in an hour and be home the same evening. Her library is the nation's; her desk is her mother's. Unsalaried and unattached, she works from that arrangement through the whole of the nineteen-twenties and thirties.
suggested_refs: The New House, Coverts Road, Claygate, Surrey, her address 1925-1981

stops.name: Chancery Lane, a document in the Public Record Office
stops.date_confidence: Publication in the first volume of the Review of English Studies is attested to 1925; the month of the archival find is unknown and defaulted to mid-year.
stops.campa: In a bundle of state papers at the Public Record Office she finds a document about English actors playing in Paris during Shakespeare's lifetime, and writes it up for the first volume of the Review of English Studies. The Times Literary Supplement notices the new and lively light it throws on Elizabethan drama. She is twenty-five and has published in her first year out of the examination hall. A second article follows two years later, out of the same class of documents.
suggested_refs: Frances A. Yates, 'English Actors in Paris during the Lifetime of Shakespeare', Review of English Studies 1 (1925)

stops.name: Canons Park, French at North London Collegiate
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the post 1929-1934; the September start is inferred from the school year. Coordinate corrected to the Canons Drive campus per OSM; the research pool's 51.6115,-0.2775 sits 1.23 km south-east. Trapp's aunt's bequest is not independently verified.
stops.campa: She teaches French at North London Collegiate School, on and off, for five years. It is the only salaried work she will hold until she is forty-one, and she resents every hour of it, because the hours come out of the reading. A modest legacy from an aunt eases the household; the rest of her income is nothing at all. In the evenings and on the train she is writing a life of John Florio out of Public Record Office documents that nobody has thought to connect to each other.
suggested_refs: North London Collegiate School, Canons Park, Edgware
sources: University of London archival fonds description for the Yates papers

stops.name: Cambridge, John Florio
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested; month unknown. The Rose Mary Crawshay Prize is misdated to 1934 in the research pool: the British Academy awarded it for John Florio in 1937. Coordinate is Cambridge, the press's city, not a building.
stops.campa: Cambridge University Press publishes her first book, subsidized, on John Florio: an Italian teaching Italian in Shakespeare's London, translator of Montaigne, a foreigner at the centre of the English literary language. Desmond MacCarthy, Harold Nicolson and Mario Praz all praise it, and three years later the British Academy gives it the Rose Mary Crawshay Prize. Asked long afterwards what all the work had been aimed at, she names a book on Shakespeare she never wrote.
stops.quote: It's all aimed at Willie, you know
stops.quote_source: Yates's own facetious remark about her life's work aiming at a book on Shakespeare she never wrote, in J. B. Trapp, 'Frances Amelia Yates 1899-1981', Proceedings of the British Academy 120 (2003), p. 531
suggested_refs: Frances A. Yates, John Florio: The Life of an Italian in Shakespeare's England (Cambridge, 1934)

stops.name: Girton College, the Italian course
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the course to summer 1935; the research pool's chronology lens gives 1936, which is wrong. July is inferred from summer.
stops.campa: She spends several weeks of the summer at Girton on a course in Italian laid on for scholars, and comes away with the language and with two friendships that last, Nesca Robb and Linetta de Castelvecchio. Italian is the door. Everything after the Florio book runs through it or through Latin read with Italian eyes: the Valois tapestries, Giulio Camillo's wooden theatre, Bruno's dialogues printed in London under a false imprint, the diagrams of a Majorcan layman dead six hundred years.
suggested_refs: Girton College, Cambridge, and its 1935 summer course in Italian for scholars

stops.name: Cambridge, A Study of Love's Labour's Lost
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested; month unknown. Empson's review is dated September 1936 in Trapp's footnote.
stops.campa: Cambridge publishes A Study of Love's Labour's Lost, in which she reads the comedy against the French academies and the learned quarrels of the fifteen-nineties and puts living men behind the play's schoolmaster and its braggart. William Empson reviews it in Life and Letters Today. She is thirty-six. He calls the argument wandering but fascinating and its biographical identifications very doubtful. Reviewers repeat both halves of that verdict for the next forty years.
stops.quote_source: William Empson, review in Life and Letters Today, Sept. 1936, p. 204, quoted in J. B. Trapp, Proceedings of the British Academy 120 (2003), p. 531; the paired verdict 'very doubtful' falls on p. 532
suggested_refs: Frances A. Yates, A Study of Love's Labour's Lost (Cambridge, 1936)

stops.name: Par, the house party and Edgar Wind
stops.date_confidence: The house party at Par and the introduction to Wind by Dorothea Waley Singer are attested verbatim by Wikipedia; the late-1936 dating is Trapp's alone. Coordinate corrected to Par per OSM at 50.3494,-4.7051; the research pool's 50.3417,-4.7053 sits 0.86 km south.
stops.campa: Dorothea Waley Singer, herself at work on Bruno, invites her to a weekend house party at Par on the Cornish coast. Another guest is Edgar Wind, deputy director of a German library three years out of Hamburg and now in London. He has her Love's Labour's Lost in his hands. Writing the scene down half a century later, in old age, she will not say outright that he was reading it, and the reservation stays in the sentence where she felt it. Within a year she is coming in to work in his library on Millbank.
stops.quote: which he appeared to be studying
stops.quote_source: Frances A. Yates, 'Autobiographical Fragments', in Ideas and Ideals in the North European Renaissance: Collected Essays III (London, 1984), p. 313, quoted in Trapp, PBA 120 (2003), p. 535
suggested_refs: Dorothea Waley Singer's house at Par, Cornwall

stops.name: Millbank, the library in exile
stops.date_confidence: Her informal association with the Institute is dated 1936/37 and cannot be fixed more closely; the library left Thames House for South Kensington during 1937, so this stop sits at the end of the Millbank years. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from aby_warburg.journey.json, whose stop 'London, Thames House on Millbank' gives 51.4959,-0.1257; the research pool's geography lens gives 51.4928,-0.1259, which is not used.
stops.campa: The Warburg library, shipped out of Hamburg in two steamers in December 1933, stands on the ground floor of Thames House on Millbank, reshelved on Aby Warburg's own principle of the good neighbour, the book you need set beside the book you asked for. Yates begins coming in. She is an unaffiliated scholar with two books and no post, sitting in a refugee institution among Germans who address one another as Professor, and she attends the Wednesday evening lectures with a private and entirely unforgiving judgement.
stops.quote_source: Yates's private verdict on an eminent historian of cosmology after a Wednesday lecture at the Warburg, quoted in Trapp, PBA 120 (2003), p. 530
suggested_refs: Thames House, Millbank, first London address of the Warburg library

stops.name: South Kensington, a lecture to five people in the blackout
stops.date_confidence: Trapp dates the lecture to 1940 without a month; day and month defaulted. The audience of fewer than half a dozen and the unheated unlit hall are Trapp's account, tagged R in the research pool.
stops.campa: Fritz Saxl and Edgar Wind ask her to lecture on the French academies. The Institute has moved to the Imperial Institute buildings in South Kensington, London is being bombed nightly, the hall is unheated and unlit, and fewer than half a dozen people come. She gives the lecture to the six of them in the dark. The lectures become the book, and the book will carry 1947 on its title page and reach the shops in 1948, held back by a shortage of paper and of money that outlasts the war.
suggested_refs: The Warburg Institute at the Imperial Institute buildings, South Kensington, 1937-1958

stops.name: South Kensington, Editor of Publications
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by Trapp and Wikipedia; month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Fritz Saxl makes her the Institute's Editor of Publications, part-time and badly paid. She is forty-one. It is the first salaried post of her adult life that is not schoolteaching, and it puts her inside the building rather than at a reader's desk within it. She edits other people's books, sees the Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes through the press, and finishes writing her own. Nine years pass in that arrangement before the Institute calls her a Lecturer, and she is fifty when it does.
suggested_refs: Fritz Saxl, director of the Warburg Institute, who created the post

segments.name: The French Academies and the Two Arts

stops.name: South Kensington, The French Academies
stops.date_confidence: The title page reads 1947; Trapp states the book actually appeared early in 1948. The February dating is an ordering device, not attested. The Institute's 1944 incorporation into the University of London, which Yates lived through in this building, is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: The French Academies of the Sixteenth Century appears with 1947 on its title page: a study of Baif's Academy of Poetry and Music and of the attempt to hold together a country tearing itself apart over religion by means of measured verse, measured music and ceremony. Four years earlier the library she wrote it in had been incorporated into the University of London and become the Warburg Institute in law as well as in fact. In her preface she says where the book was composed, and she means the London of 1940 exactly.
stops.quote: the atmosphere in which the French academies of the sixteenth century first presented themselves as a steadying subject in a disintegrating world
stops.quote_source: Frances A. Yates, The French Academies of the Sixteenth Century (London, 1947 [1948]), p. v, quoted in Trapp, PBA 120 (2003), p. 534
suggested_refs: Frances A. Yates, The French Academies of the Sixteenth Century (Warburg Institute, 1947)

stops.name: South Kensington, Gombrich puts Camillo in her hands
stops.date_confidence: Trapp dates both the Camillo book and the lectureship to 1950 without months; tagged R in the research pool for the Camillo episode. Day and month defaulted.
stops.campa: Ernst Gombrich puts a small Venetian book into her hands: Giulio Camillo's Idea del theatro, the description of a wooden amphitheatre built in the fifteen-thirties whose tiers held not spectators but images, each image a compartment of the whole of knowledge, the man in the middle looking out at everything that can be known. She is fifty, and the Camillo material holds her for the thirty-one years she has left. Trapp, writing the memoir long afterwards, says this is the book that made the difference.
stops.quote_source: Yates's own description of her method, quoted in Trapp, PBA 120 (2003), p. 528, as a general characterization rather than a remark about any one subject
suggested_refs: Giulio Camillo, L'Idea del Theatro (Florence and Venice, 1550)

stops.name: Claygate, two deaths in the house
stops.date_confidence: Sources conflict and the conflict is left standing: Wikipedia gives March 1951 for her sister Hannah's death from leukaemia, the dossier gives 22 October 1951 and cites a certified death entry. The mother's death in October 1952 is confirmed by Wikipedia. The March dating is used here for ordering only.
stops.campa: Her sister Hannah dies of leukaemia in the house at Coverts Road, and her mother dies the following October. The household that had carried her since Southsea, that had moved her from dockyard to dockyard, paid for the correspondence courses and put everything it had left onto her after Jimmy, comes down to Frances and her surviving sister Ruby. She is fifty-two. She goes on taking the train up to London, and the notebooks from these years are as full as any she keeps.
suggested_refs: The Yates family papers and diaries in the Warburg Institute Archive
sources: Research dossier chronology, unconfirmed on the October dating

stops.name: Rome, Campo de' Fiori
stops.date_confidence: The September 1951 journey through Italy to sites associated with Giordano Bruno is attested by Wikipedia; the particular stop in the Campo de' Fiori is tradition and inference, tagged R, as is the Nola visit folded into this campa. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from giordano_bruno.journey.json, stop 'Rome, Campo de' Fiori, the fire'.
stops.campa: She travels through Italy in September to the places where Giordano Bruno lived and was burned. In the Campo de' Fiori the market runs as it always runs, and Ettore Ferrari's hooded bronze stands in the middle of it facing the Vatican, raised in 1889 by Italians who wanted a martyr for free thought. Yates is not looking for that Bruno. She has begun to suspect that the man burned on this square was a magus, and that the nineteenth century's philosopher of science is a costume put on a Hermetic priest. She goes south to Nola as well, to the town he came from.
suggested_refs: Ettore Ferrari's 1889 bronze of Giordano Bruno on the Campo de' Fiori
Nola, Campania, Bruno's birthplace

stops.name: South Kensington, the art of Ramon Lull
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested; month unknown. The 1960 sequel article proposing Erigena is folded into this stop's campa and is attested for that year.
stops.campa: The Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes prints her essay on the art of Ramon Llull, approached through his theory of the elements: the revolving figures, the letters B to K, the combinatory wheels a Majorcan layman devised in the thirteenth century to convert the world by demonstration rather than by argument. Trapp calls it the hardest thing she ever set herself. She comes back to it six years later with a second article putting Erigena's Neoplatonism behind the Art, and she ends the first one by refusing to conclude.
stops.quote: This article has concluded nothing, for it is not an end but a beginning.... My aim has been to re-open the problem of Ramon Lull and his Art through suggesting some fresh ways of approaching the problem.
stops.quote_source: Frances A. Yates, 'The Art of Ramon Lull', Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes 17 (1954), reprinted in Lull and Bruno: Collected Essays I (London, 1982), pp. 66-7, quoted in Trapp, PBA 120 (2003), p. 541
suggested_refs: Frances A. Yates, 'The Art of Ramon Lull: An Approach to It through Lull's Theory of the Elements', JWCI 17 (1954)

stops.name: South Kensington, the memory theatre lectures
stops.date_confidence: The 1952 lecture on Bruno and artificial memory, the 1955 lecture on Camillo's theatre, and the 1955 essay in the volume for Bruno Nardi are all reported by Trapp and tagged R in the research pool; they are compressed into one stop dated to the later year.
stops.campa: She lectures at the Institute on Bruno and artificial memory, then on Camillo's theatre, and publishes an essay on the Ciceronian art of memory in a volume for Bruno Nardi. The classical technique is simple and very old: fix a building in the mind, walk its rooms in order, set at each place a striking image carrying what is to be said. Cicero has it; Quintilian has it. When the imagined building stopped being a device for orators and became a plan of the universe, and why, is the question she has now set herself.
suggested_refs: The Rhetorica ad Herennium and the classical art of places and images

segments.name: Woburn Square and the Hermetic Tradition

stops.name: Woburn Square, the Institute's own building
stops.date_confidence: The move to the Holden building is attested to 1958 and her promotion to Reader to 1956; month unknown. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from aby_warburg.journey.json, stop 'London, Woburn Square'; the research pool's geography and afterlife lenses give 51.5222,-0.1298 and 51.5225,-0.1296, neither used.
stops.campa: Promoted Reader two years before, she moves with the Institute into the building it has waited a quarter of a century for: Charles Holden's design on Woburn Square in Bloomsbury, four floors of stack shelved by Gertrud Bing on the founder's own arrangement, image, word, orientation, action, so that walking upward through the library is walking through an argument about how a civilization remembers. The books that came out of Hamburg in a hurry have an address of their own. Yates has a room, and works in it for the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: The Charles Holden building for the Warburg Institute, Woburn Square, opened 1958

stops.name: Woburn Square, The Valois Tapestries
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested; month unknown. The letter to Philip Hughes is undated in Trapp's account and is placed here for its subject rather than on documentary grounds.
stops.campa: The Institute publishes her book on the eight Valois tapestries in the Uffizi: court festivals woven in Flanders and read here as an argument rather than as decoration, a politique case for reconciliation made in silk for a France killing itself over religion. Writing to the Catholic historian Philip Hughes about his book on the Counter-Reformation in England, she sets out her own position in a sentence whose central joke is not offered as a joke at all.
stops.quote: an Anglican, who takes the historical view that the Nazi revolution of 1559, and all the miserable complications which ensued, deprived me of part of my natural and native inheritance as an English Catholic
stops.quote_source: Frances Yates, letter to Philip Hughes, Yates Archive, Warburg Institute, quoted in Trapp, PBA 120 (2003), p. 537
suggested_refs: The eight Valois tapestries in the Uffizi, Florence

stops.name: Woburn Square, Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested; month unknown. The Clark Library seminar of 9 March 1974 that tested the book's strong form is cited here as a source rather than staged as a stop, because Yates's own attendance at it is not attested.
stops.campa: Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition argues that Bruno is not a martyr of science but a Renaissance magus, moving in the world Ficino and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola built out of the Hermetic writings, and that the infinite universe he burned for is a religious vision before it is a cosmological one. Casaubon's 1614 redating of the Corpus Hermeticum to the second century is the hinge of the whole book, and Agrippa, John Dee and Robert Fludd are read again in its light. She writes it in under a year, on twenty years of notes.
stops.quote: that magic, astrology and myth form the core of his thinking and that it is only by working outwards from this more primitive world of powerful symbols that we can hope to understand his apparently more rational philosophical works
stops.quote_source: D. P. Walker, review of Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition, Modern Language Review 61 (1966), pp. 719-21, quoted in Trapp, PBA 120 (2003), p. 544
suggested_refs: Frances A. Yates, Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1964)
Robert S. Westman and J. E. McGuire, eds, Hermeticism and the Scientific Revolution: Papers Read at a Clark Library Seminar, March 9, 1974 (1977)

stops.name: London, The Art of Memory
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested; month unknown. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from robert_fludd.journey.json, whose stop 'London: Frances Yates and the memory theatre' pins this same event at 51.5074,-0.1278. That stop is Yates's, not Fludd's, and belongs on this file.
stops.campa: The Art of Memory traces the classical technique of places and images from the Ad Herennium through Albertus and Aquinas to Giulio Camillo's wooden theatre, Giordano Bruno's revolving seals, and the engraved memory building in Robert Fludd. In the last chapter she argues that Fludd's theatre is a real one: the stage of the Globe, drawn by a man who had stood in it. Theatre historians with no interest in Hermetic folios find themselves obliged to open one, and at least one of them gives ground on the engraving.
stops.quote_source: C. Walter Hodges, The Globe Restored. A Study of the Elizabethan Theatre, 2nd edn (London, 1968), p. 119, quoted in Trapp, PBA 120 (2003), p. 546
suggested_refs: Frances A. Yates, The Art of Memory (Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1966), chapter XVI

stops.name: Princeton, a week at the Institute for Advanced Study
stops.date_confidence: The spring 1966 American tour and its itinerary come from Trapp and are tagged R in the research pool; no stop on it was independently confirmed. The day is defaulted and the coordinate is the Institute campus.
stops.campa: The American spring tour runs from Johns Hopkins to the Folger, Bryn Mawr, Columbia, Harvard, MIT, the Newberry, Chicago and Northwestern, and closes with a week at the Institute for Advanced Study. She is sixty-six, two years past the Bruno book, and has held a salaried post of any kind for twenty-five years. Every Renaissance department on the eastern seaboard wants her in the room, and the itinerary runs solid from Baltimore to Chicago. She lectures at each place in turn, takes the week at Princeton, and goes home to Claygate.
suggested_refs: The Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, final stop of the 1966 tour

stops.name: Woburn Square, Fellow of the British Academy
stops.date_confidence: Election to the British Academy is attested to July 1967 and the retirement to the same year; the day is unknown. The D.Litt of 1965, awarded by examination on the published work, is folded into this campa, as are the Readership of 1956 and the 1962 redesignation as Reader in the History of the Renaissance, both attested by Trapp p. 529.
stops.campa: She is elected a Fellow of the British Academy in July, and in the same year reaches the Institute's retiring age and is retired from it. She is made an Honorary Fellow at once and goes on teaching and using the library exactly as before. She had been Reader since 1956, redesignated Reader in the History of the Renaissance in 1962. The London D.Litt came two years ago, awarded by examination of the published work rather than by thesis. She is sixty-seven and has never sat for a doctorate.
suggested_refs: The Fellowship of the British Academy, elected July 1967

stops.name: London, Theatre of the World
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested; month unknown. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from robert_fludd.journey.json, which uses 51.5074,-0.1278 for the Yates-Fludd Globe material. The Globe argument itself is contested and is presented here as contested.
stops.campa: Theatre of the World argues that the Elizabethan public playhouse is Vitruvian: that the proportions of the Roman theatre reached the carpenters of Shoreditch and Bankside through John Dee's preface to the English Euclid of 1570, and that Robert Fludd's engraved theatre preserves the scheme. Theatre historians object at once that Fludd's diagram was printed in 1619, twenty years after the first Globe was raised, and that a plan cannot be evidence for a building it postdates. The dispute is not settled. She does not withdraw the claim.
suggested_refs: Frances A. Yates, Theatre of the World (Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1969)

stops.date_confidence: Publication year and the OBE in the 1972 New Year Honours are both attested by Trapp; months unknown.

In the same season she puts out, with an introduction, a facsimile of Simon Bouquet's book on the entries of Charles IX and his queen into Paris: triumphal arches, allegorical figures, a whole city dressed for a few days as an argument about monarchy. She has been reading festivals as arguments since the tapestries. Bouquet's account was printed in 1572; the entries themselves took place in March 1571.

stops.name: Claygate, the willow in the garden
stops.date_confidence: The Smith College offer and her refusal are attested to February 1976 by Wikipedia. The willow's descent from the tree at Napoleon's grave on Saint Helena is a family belief reported by Trapp and is explicitly not documented; it is carried here as legend, at the Claygate pin, because the tree and the belief were both at Claygate.

The woman who has spent forty years separating traditions from their proofs keeps the tree. In February Smith College offers her its Kennedy Professorship. She is seventy-six, and she declines it.

In the same year she is appointed Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire. The external student from Worthing who never sat for a doctorate is Dame Frances Yates, and the Institute she retired from a decade earlier still keeps a room for her.

stops.name: Budapest, the last research journey
stops.date_confidence: Tagged R. The Hungarian journey of summer 1981 is the confirmed element; Budapest as the specific city is an inference from the dossier and is not independently verified. Month approximate.
stops.campa: At eighty-one she goes to Hungary, to lecture and to look at a country she has known chiefly through other people's documents. She comes back with a flat judgement: English-language scholarship on the Renaissance has been written as though Central Europe were not there. Bohemia, the Palatinate and Hungary are where the last twenty years of her work kept leading, and she has been reading their history in English libraries the whole time. It is the last journey she makes out of England.

stops.campa: Her last lecture is given in Manchester Cathedral, on John Dee, who was warden of the collegiate church that stands on this ground and whose wife Jane lies buried in it, dead of the plague in 1605. Dee had come north at sixty-eight to a foundation whose fellows cheated him over the rents and whose accounts never added up, and held the office in name until he left it.
